title: Your launch is going to slip and you have to say so
summary: Six weeks became ten. Three audiences, one message, and a strong temptation to wait one more week before telling anyone.

brief.role: You are the PM for a team building a new client portal.
brief.company: Brightmoor, a 90-person company selling case-management software to law firms.
brief.context: The client portal was scheduled to launch in two weeks. This morning the team confirmed that authentication work discovered in testing adds about four weeks, putting launch at six weeks out. Three customers have been told the original date, one of whom has scheduled internal training for launch week. Your VP has been reporting green status to the executive team for a month based on your updates. The weekly status email goes out tomorrow morning.
brief.objective: Communicate the slip in a way that preserves trust and lets people act on it.
brief.constraints: The four-week estimate is the engineering lead's, with a stated range of three to five weeks. You cannot compress it meaningfully without cutting the audit-log requirement, which two of the three customers need for compliance.
brief.task: Decide what you communicate, to whom, and when.

evidenceCards.title: What changed and how confident the estimate is
evidenceCards.content:
From the engineering lead:
'The portal has to authenticate users who are not employees of our customers — their clients. We assumed we could reuse the staff identity system. In testing we found it grants implicit access to case metadata that external users must not see, so we need a separate identity path with its own permission model.

Four weeks is my estimate. Three if the permission model is as simple as I think, five if the audit-log requirement means we also have to rework how we log access. I will know which by the end of next week.

What we cannot do is ship without it. That is not a schedule risk, it is a data-exposure risk.'

Removing the audit log would save roughly one week. Two of the three pilot customers have named it as a compliance requirement.

evidenceCards.title: Who is affected and how
evidenceCards.content:
Three pilot customers:
- Halloran & Wise: has booked internal training for launch week, 40 people, and a trainer is contracted. Cancelling with more than three weeks' notice costs nothing; inside three weeks it costs them a fee.
- Deswick LLP: no dependencies named. Their sponsor asks for a written update monthly and is generally relaxed.
- Marchmont: has told their own largest client the portal is coming 'this quarter'. Six weeks is still inside the quarter, by nine days.

Internally:
- Your VP has reported green for four weeks and presents to the executive team on Thursday.
- Sales has two opportunities where the portal is part of the pitch, with demos scheduled in three and five weeks.
- The support team has drafted help content against the original date.

The engineering lead's team has not been told the date is public.

evidenceCards.title: Context on how updates land here
evidenceCards.content:
Your VP, in a one-to-one two months ago: 'I do not mind bad news. I mind finding out from somebody else, and I mind hearing about a problem at the same time as I hear it is unfixable.'

The previous PM on this product had a launch slip twice, each time announced about a week before the original date. The second time, one customer escalated to the CEO. The team's credibility with the pilot customers is described by the account team as 'recovering'.

A colleague's advice this morning: 'Wait until end of next week when the estimate firms up. Then you can tell them four weeks or six weeks instead of a range, and you only have one awkward conversation instead of two.'

The status email template has a red/amber/green field, a summary line, and a section for changes since last week.

decisionPrompt: What do you do about communicating the slip?

decisionOptions.label: Tell everyone now, with the range and a date for the firm estimate
decisionOptions.description: Brief your VP today before the status email, move the status to red with the reason, call Halloran & Wise before their three-week cancellation deadline, and commit to a firm date at the end of next week.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Your VP is not pleased about the slip and is visibly relieved to hear it before Thursday rather than during. She asks two questions about the data-exposure finding and adopts your framing for the executive update.
Halloran & Wise cancel their training at no cost and reschedule. Their programme manager thanks you for the notice. Marchmont confirms six weeks still works for their client commitment. Deswick acknowledges by email.
Sales moves one demo and keeps the other, using the current build.
At the end of the following week the estimate firms at four weeks and you send a short confirmation. The second conversation is a non-event because it was expected.
Trade-off: you communicated an uncertain number and spent a week holding a range in public, in exchange for everyone being able to act while it was still cheap.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale ties the timing to the customer's three-week cancellation window and the VP's Thursday presentation, and treats a stated range with a firm-up date as more honest than a false single number.

decisionOptions.label: Wait until the estimate firms up next week
decisionOptions.description: Hold the status at amber, tell nobody outside the team yet, and communicate a single confident date in eight days.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The estimate firms at four weeks as expected and you send a clear, confident update eight days later.
By then Halloran & Wise are inside their three-week window and pay the trainer's cancellation fee. Their programme manager asks when you knew. Your VP has presented green to the executive team on Thursday and finds out on the following Monday, which is the specific thing she told you she minds.
The update itself is well written and lands badly, because the question everyone asks is not 'how long' but 'how long did you know'.
Trade-off: you bought a cleaner message and paid with the week in which the information was still useful to other people.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak. It optimises the message at the expense of the audience's ability to act, and walks directly into the VP's stated concern and the team's credibility history.

decisionOptions.label: Cut the audit log to save a week and communicate a shorter slip
decisionOptions.description: Drop the audit-log requirement, bring the slip to three weeks, and present that as the plan.
decisionOptions.consequence:
You take the proposal to the account team, who point out that two of the three pilot customers named the audit log as a compliance requirement. One of them would not be able to go live without it.
The idea is dropped after two days, during which nobody was told about the slip. You then communicate a five-week slip in a week where the customer's training cancellation window has closed.
Trade-off: you spent the most valuable days looking for a smaller number to report, and reported a worse one later.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Low. It sacrifices a stated compliance requirement to shrink a number, and the delay it causes is more costly than the week it would have saved.

decisionOptions.label: Brief your VP now and hold the customer conversations until the estimate firms
decisionOptions.description: Protect your VP from being surprised on Thursday, but wait to give customers a single firm date.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Your VP is briefed before Thursday and handles the executive update well. That part works.
Halloran & Wise are told eight days later, inside their cancellation window, and pay the fee. The account manager, who also was not told, learns about the slip from the customer.
In the retro your VP notes that the internal handling was right and asks why the same logic did not apply to the customer who had the earliest decision to make.
Trade-off: you correctly protected one relationship and applied the reasoning to only one of your audiences.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Partial credit for correct instinct on the internal audience. Mark down for not extending the same reasoning to the customer facing a dated, costed decision.

rubric.referenceReasoning: The value of a schedule update is not accuracy, it is whether the recipient can still act on it. Halloran & Wise can cancel training for free with more than three weeks' notice and the slip puts them right at that boundary, so a week of delay converts a free decision into a paid one. Your VP has stated her own condition explicitly — not finding out from somebody else, not hearing about a problem at the same time as hearing it is unfixable — and she presents on Thursday. A range with a date for the firm number is more honest than a single number invented for tidiness, and the engineering lead has given a clear, defensible reason the work cannot be cut: it is a data-exposure risk, not a schedule preference. The audit log is a compliance requirement for two of three pilots, so trading it for a week is not available. A strong answer sequences the audiences by how soon each has a decision to make, says what is known and what is not, and commits to when the uncertainty resolves.
evidenceSignals: Notices Halloran & Wise's three-week free cancellation window

Uses the VP's stated preference about how she wants bad news
Recognises the audit log is a compliance requirement for two of three pilots
Uses the previous PM's late-slip history as context for how this will be received
Treats three-to-five weeks as information to share rather than to resolve privately

Lets the VP present green after the team knows otherwise

learnTakeaway.title: Communicate on the recipient's clock, not on yours
learnTakeaway.body: The instinct to wait for a firm number is about wanting a clean message. But a schedule update is only worth anything while the recipient can still change what they do with it, and their decision deadlines are rarely the same as your estimate's. Work out who has to decide something and when, then say what you know, what you do not, and when you will know it. A range delivered in time is more useful, and reads as more honest, than a precise number delivered after the decision has already been made.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: Communicate today, with the range. The deciding factor isn't my comfort with the number — it's that other people have earlier deadlines than my estimate does. Halloran & Wise can cancel 40 people of training free with over three weeks' notice, and the slip puts them right on that line. And my VP presents Thursday having reported green for a month; she told me what she minds is finding out from someone else. So: brief her this morning, move the status to red with a firm-date commitment for end of next week, and call Halloran & Wise and Marchmont today with the account manager.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: I'd brief my VP and the account team today and hold the direct customer calls for four days, until the engineering lead knows whether the audit-log rework is needed. This product's credibility with these three pilots is recovering after two late slips, and 'somewhere between three and five weeks' risks reading as another PM who doesn't know what's happening. Four days gets a firm number without waiting eight, and it still leaves Halloran & Wise inside their free cancellation window — I checked that before choosing to wait. If it hasn't firmed by Thursday, I call all three.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: The estimate is three to five weeks and we will know which by the end of next week. I would keep the status at amber and wait, because telling people a range now and a different number in eight days means two difficult conversations and makes us look like we do not have control of the project. One clear message is better than two vague ones.
